opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing that worries me most is the tendency to collapse a whole distribution down to a single number. You'll hear someone say "my timeline is 2032," and it gets repeated as if that's the forecast. But what really matters for decision-making is the shape of the distribution, and in particular how much probability sits in the early years. If you've got a median of, say, fifteen years out, but a long right tail, that can still mean a ten or twenty percent chance that it arrives within five years. That's a very different situation from a tight distribution around fifteen years, and it calls for very different actions.

A related issue is that people often argue about medians when the policy-relevant question is about the tails. If you're thinking about whether institutions are prepared, whether safety research is mature enough, or whether governance mechanisms exist, then a meaningful chance of very short timelines should dominate your planning, even if it isn't your central estimate. We do this naturally in other domains. You don't buy fire insurance because you expect your house to burn down this year.

I also worry about how forecasts get anchored to recent news. When there's a striking capability release, timelines contract sharply in public discussion; when progress seems to plateau for a few months, people swing the other way. Some updating is warranted, but much of it is just salience. A good forecast should be relatively stable unless you've learned something structural, like how compute scaling is going, or whether a key bottleneck has been removed.

And finally, there's the definitional slipperiness. "Transformative AI," "AGI," "human-level AI": these get used interchangeably, but they pick out quite different thresholds. Two people can appear to disagree by a decade when really they're forecasting different events. So before arguing about dates, I'd encourage people to be explicit about what milestone they mean and what it would look like in the world. That alone would clear up a surprising amount of apparent disagreement.

r001.rationale: The response discusses forecast distributions, tails, news-driven updates, and milestone definitions, but does not say forecasts estimate when transformative AI could be built under business-as-usual conditions.

r002.rationale: It does not mention a moratorium or concern that a delay beyond the predicted date might leave a forecast unrefuted.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that worries me most is that we tend to talk about these forecasts as if they were a single number, when really what we have is a very wide distribution, and the shape of that distribution matters enormously for what we should do.

So someone will say "I think transformative AI arrives in 2035," and that gets repeated as if it's a point estimate, a date you could put in a calendar. But if you actually sit down with the people making these forecasts, what they'll tell you is something more like: there's maybe a ten or fifteen percent chance it happens within five years, and a substantial chance it's decades away, and a real tail where it's much further out than anyone's currently discussing. The median gets quoted, and all of that structure gets lost.

And that matters because the policy implications of a fat left tail are completely different from the implications of the median. If there's even a modest probability of something transformative happening very soon, that justifies a lot of preparation now, regardless of where the median sits. People who disagree about the median can often agree about the tail, and the tail is where most of the action is.

The second thing I'd say is that I think we conflate several different events under this one phrase. When is AI going to be economically transformative, in the sense of doubling growth rates? When is it going to be strategically transformative, in the sense of mattering for the balance of power between nations? When does it become capable of doing AI research itself, which would change the dynamics of further progress? And when does it become dangerous in the sense that existential risk people care about? These could easily be separated by years or decades, and they have quite different warning signs. Asking "when does transformative AI arrive?" as a single question tends to blur all of that together.

And then there's a subtler problem, which is that these forecasts are not independent of the forecasting. If a lot of serious people say it's coming in ten years, that shifts investment, it shifts talent, it shifts what governments do. So the forecasts are partly self-fulfilling and partly self-defeating, and I don't think our methodology handles that well at all. We're mostly borrowing tools built for predicting things that don't care whether they're being predicted.

So I'm not against forecasting. I think it's really important work. But I'd like us to be more honest that what we're producing is a wide, lumpy distribution over several different events, rather than a date, and to make our decisions with that whole shape in view.

astra-6.text:
What worries me is that we tend to frame this as a question about a date: when will transformative AI arrive? And then we talk about people with short timelines or long timelines, as though everyone has a particular year in mind and the disagreement is just about which year it is.

But what we really need is a probability distribution. Someone might think the most likely outcome is that it takes many decades, while still assigning a substantial probability to it happening in the next few years. Those aren’t contradictory beliefs. And for deciding how urgently we should prepare, that probability of an early arrival can matter a great deal.

If you ask someone for their median estimate—the date by which they think there’s a fifty percent chance—and that date is quite far away, it can sound reassuring. But it doesn’t tell you how much probability they assign to arrival before we’re ready. You could agree about the median and disagree enormously about that.

So I’d like us to spend less time treating forecasts as appointments in the calendar, and more time asking what range of possibilities we need to be prepared for. Uncertainty about the date isn’t a reason to assume we have plenty of time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses date-based forecasts, probability distributions, and early-arrival risk, but does not say that forecasts estimate when AI could be built under business-as-usual conditions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a moratorium or concern that delaying AI beyond a forecasted date would leave the forecast unrefuted.

sol-6.1.text:
One thing that worries me is that people often talk about a date as though it were a deadline. They’ll say, “I think transformative AI will arrive in 2040,” and then the conversation proceeds as if we have until 2040 to get ready. But that date might be the middle of their probability distribution. They might think there’s a substantial chance it happens much sooner.

For questions of preparedness, that earlier possibility matters a great deal. If you thought there was a 10% chance of something enormously consequential happening within five years, you wouldn’t normally ignore it just because your best guess was twenty years away.

I’d much rather hear people describe their uncertainty: how much probability they put on the next five years, the next ten years, and on it taking much longer. That also helps us distinguish disagreement about the most likely outcome from disagreement about what we ought to do. You can have quite long timelines as your central estimate and still think that preparing now is extremely important.
